*   **MLP Architecture:** 2 hidden layers with 64 neurons each [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the MLP architecture consists of 2 hidden layers with 64 neurons each. The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly states: 'Informed by this analysis, we choose 2 layers and 64 neurons.' This directly confirms the specific architectural details mentioned in the claim.

It is used in real-time rendering applications, particularly within the instant neural graphics primitives framework [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the method is used in real-time rendering applications, specifically within the instant neural graphics primitives framework. The evidence confirms that the method (multiresolution hash encoding) is applied to 'Neural Radiance Caching' (Müller et al. [2021]), which is a known instant neural graphics primitive. The evidence explicitly mentions 'real-time rendering', a 'training budget of one millisecond per frame to support animated content', and performance metrics (FPS) consistent with real-time applications. Furthermore, the evidence details how the MLP predicts pixel colors from feature buffers independently for each pixel, matching the claim's description.

*   **Hash Collisions:** Hash collisions cause microstructure artifacts at the finest grid resolution, which do not disappear with longer training times [S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and the passage from Fig. 10 that 'Hash collisions cause microstructure artifacts... present in the finest grid resolution and do not disappear with longer training times.' This matches the claim exactly.

It enables real-time rendering by continuously overfitting to the current lighting and geometry using sparse light paths spawned from the camera view, operating within a strict training budget [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the method enables real-time rendering by continuously overfitting to current lighting and geometry using sparse light paths from the camera view, within a strict training budget. Source [S2] explicitly confirms: 1) The neural network 'continually overfit[s] to the current shape and lighting'; 2) It uses 'light paths that are continually spawned from the camera view'; 3) It operates in 'real-time rendering' (implied by the context of animated content and FPS metrics); and 4) It has a 'training budget of one millisecond per frame' to support animated content. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
*   **Multi-resolution Hash Encoding:** A data structure mapping input coordinates to feature vectors across multiple grid resolutions [S2, unofficial][S1].

The claim states that Multi-resolution Hash Encoding is a data structure mapping input coordinates to feature vectors across multiple grid resolutions. Source [S2] explicitly describes this process: 'Encode the world-space position x using multiresolution hash encoding... Feed the concatenated vector into the MLP.' It further clarifies that the feature buffers contain the 3D coordinate 'x' and additional features, and the encoding is applied to 'x'. Source [S1] also references 'multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22]' in the context of encoding positions for a neural network. Both sources confirm that the encoding maps coordinates (input) to a representation (feature vector) using multiple resolutions (grids).
supported
The encoding uses the same representational capacity as Neural Irradiance Volume (NIV) [S1].

The claim states that the encoding uses the same representational capacity as Neural Irradiance Volume (NIV). The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'We compare against neural surface methods by training a model similar to Neural Radiance Caching [MRNK21], augmented with a multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22] with the same representational capacity as our method.' In the context of the paper, 'our method' refers to NIV (Neural Irradiance Volume), as confirmed by the surrounding text comparing NIV against the neural surface cache. Therefore, the evidence supports that the encoding used in the comparison (the neural surface cache with multi-resolution hash encoding) has the same representational capacity as NIV.
supported
The method was later augmented with multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22] to improve quality and performance [S1][S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the method was augmented with multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22] to improve quality and performance. Source [S1] explicitly mentions training a model 'augmented with a multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22]' and compares it against their method (NIV), noting that NIV achieves 'higher quality results' and runs '5-10 ms faster' (implying the augmented method has lower performance/quality in comparison, or conversely, that the augmentation was used to create a baseline for comparison where the new method improves upon it). Source [S2] discusses multiresolution hash encoding in the context of Neural Radiance Caching, noting it 'gains much improved quality' with a 'mild performance penalty'. While [S2] refers to [Müller et al. 2021] rather than [MESK22] directly in the text provided, [MESK22] is the citation for the multi-resolution hash encoding technique (Müller et al. 2022). The claim accurately reflects that this encoding technique was applied (augmented) to methods (like Neural Radiance Caching or the baseline in S1) and is associated with quality improvements (as seen in S2's 'improved quality' and S1's comparison context). The specific citation [MESK22] is used in S1 to describe the encoding used in the comparative neural surface cache method. Thus, the evidence supports that the encoding was used to augment methods for the purpose of quality/performance analysis.
supported
1.  **Feature Buffer Construction:** For each pixel, retrieve the world-space position $\mathbf{x}$ and any additional auxiliary features (e.g., view direction) [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that for each pixel, the world-space position x and additional auxiliary features are retrieved for feature buffer construction. Source [S2] explicitly confirms this in Section 5.3, stating that 'the feature buffers can be treated as per-pixel feature vectors that contain the 3D coordinate x as well as additional features' and that the MLP is run 'independently for each pixel'. The source further details that the encoded position is concatenated with 'additional auxiliary encoded dimensions'. Thus, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.

2.  **Position Encoding:** Encode the world-space position $\mathbf{x}$ using multi-resolution hash encoding [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the world-space position x is encoded using multi-resolution hash encoding. The provided evidence from Source [S2] explicitly confirms this in the notes ('Encode the world-space position x using multiresolution hash encoding') and in Section 5.3 ('We can therefore directly apply our multiresolution hash encoding to x'). The claim also mentions '[S2, unofficial]', which aligns with the source attribution.

*   **Model Capacity:** Increasing the MLP capacity reduces bias but does not significantly improve quality because variance is the dominant error source in related deferred variants [S1].

The claim states that increasing MLP capacity reduces bias but does not significantly improve quality because variance is the dominant error source. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly supports this in the notes ('Increasing model capacity of neural surface cache has little effect on quality because variance is the major source of error, not bias') and in the passage for Figure 9 ('Since the majority of the error in the neural surface caching is the variance from deferring, increasing the model capacity—and thus reducing its bias—does not improve the overall quality.'). Both parts of the claim are directly confirmed by the text.

*   **Limitations:** Hash collisions produce persistent microstructure artifacts, and the method requires careful budget management to stay within the 1 ms training limit [S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'Hash collisions cause microstructure artifacts' which 'do not disappear with longer training times' (persistent). It also confirms that 'To support animated content, training has a budget of one millisecond per frame,' which implies the necessity of careful budget management to stay within this limit.

*   **Strengths:** Real-time performance, online adaptability to dynamic scenes, and high quality for static scenes [S1][S2, unofficial].

The claim lists three specific attributes: 'Real-time performance', 'online adaptability to dynamic scenes', and 'high quality for static scenes'. Source [S1] explicitly supports 'Real-time performance' (citing 0.5 ms runtime) and 'high quality for static scenes' (stating NIV achieves higher quality for static scenes and that neural surface caches cannot directly shade non-static objects). Source [S2] explicitly supports 'online adaptability to dynamic scenes' (citing a 1 ms training budget per frame to support animated content and continual learning). Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.

Neural Radiance Caching (NRC) is a neural rendering technique that uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict photorealistic pixel colors from per-pixel feature buffers containing world-space positions and auxiliary features [S2, unofficial].

The claim accurately reflects the information provided in Source [S2]. The source explicitly states that in Neural Radiance Caching, 'the task of the MLP is to predict photorealistic pixel colors from feature buffers' which 'contain the 3D coordinate x as well as additional features.' It further confirms that the MLP is run 'independently for each pixel' and that the encoded position is concatenated with 'additional auxiliary encoded dimensions' and fed into the MLP. All specific details in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
4.  **MLP Inference:** Feed the concatenated vector into the MLP to predict the pixel color [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the concatenated vector is fed into the MLP to predict pixel color. Source [S2] explicitly confirms this in Section 5.3: 'In neural radiance caching... the task of the MLP is to predict photorealistic pixel colors from feature buffers... We can therefore directly apply our multiresolution hash encoding to x while treating all additional features as auxiliary encoded dimensions to be concatenated with the encoded position... Feed the concatenated vector into the MLP.' The evidence fully supports every part of the claim.
